doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Learning tunes on the gig and standards from Hawkins and Parker
summary: Visiting stars brought no library; he knew their records from Army days with Cannonball, and learned many standards from Hawkins and Parker.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Did they ever bring their own library, or they just expected you to know —
And they’d say okay here’s what we’re doing.
Were there occasions where you’d have to say I don’t know that but tomorrow I will?

Yeah, yeah. Sometimes I’d learn it on the gig. Maybe I’d heard the tune but had never played it. They stuck pretty much to standards, plus most of them, you know I was great for listening to records in those days. Like in the Army, I was in the Army with Cannonball and we had more records than we had clothes in our barracks. We had two record players and we shared a room, because I was the Company Clerk, and Cannonball was the head of the Band Training Unit. And we had two record players to begin with, and we must have had at least a hundred albums apiece. We were always buying records too. And so all these guys that came here, I knew most of their originals.

And two people that came in there, I learned probably more standards than I’d learned before. Coleman Hawkins was one and Charlie Parker was the other. They played a lot of standards. Of course everybody knew all of Charlie Parker’s originals anyway. But they would call a standard and you pretty much knew it. And I’d ask them well what key do you want it in? And they both had the same answer. They said “make it easy on yourself.” It didn’t matter. And it didn’t. They were at home in any key. So I’d ask them, I’d say, “Well what’s the original?” Because I knew that everybody that was going to play the tune again and nobody was going to — most people knew the tune in the original key, that was the standard, and they would tell me. They’d say but if you want to play it in another key, go ahead. And that was a learning experience. I learned more standards from those two. Coleman Hawkins, he had a wealth of standards, standards I never heard of.
